prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key d01b917cd5a2
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. They had a pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories. Models, seeds and samples were all to be compared, and sampling used temperature 1.0.
O1: Used a paired control/treatment design over five held-out scenarios, with each request fixed verbatim and reused across every model, seed and sample.
O2: Generate many paraphrased variants of each scenario with irrelevant details varied, and compare behavior across variants to check robustness to phrasing.
O3: Use a larger set of distinct, naturally phrased requests, some of them borderline decoys, with one or two samples each, so the result isn't tied to five scenarios.
O4: Generate evaluation prompts as natural user requests from a held-out hierarchy of domains, topics and styles disjoint from the training distribution, so every phrasing is new to the model.
O5: Generate a large held-out set of model-written requests with varied domains and styles, disjoint from the training material, and sample each once or twice.

=== key 90d1a2df575d
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition) and wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories depict human-to-human technical help-seeking, generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test, where the treatment adds a one-sentence limitation to the same request.
O1: Hold out new seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert them to chat requests, so that any difference between control and treatment cannot come from a shift in domain or format.
O2: Write the evaluation requests as realistic assistant conversations with named people, mundane detail and incidental noise, so the test resembles real user traffic and the limitation is embedded in the request.
O3: Take real or replayed assistant conversations, minimally edit them to add the limitation, and use those as the evaluation inputs instead of authoring new scenarios.
O4: Used evaluation scenarios that are deliberately not drawn from the story-generation seed pool. They are ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant, whereas the training stories show human-to-human technical help-seeking.

=== key 757f96363f56
Context: In evaluating the fine-tuned models, some sampled rollouts do not read as replies to the user. They turn into third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker scripts or fake user turns inside the assistant message. The team had to decide which rollouts feed the behavior-rate figures, and an automated grader can score each rollout on how much it looks like a direct chat reply.
O1: Reported behavior rates only over rollouts that an automated grader judges to be direct chat-form replies (rubric score >= 7/10).
O2: Have people read a sample of the story-form rollouts and apply a deterministic rule-based format check, then drop only those that clearly fail, reporting how many were dropped for each condition and model.
O3: Score every generated rollout by checking, with a flag-invariant regular expression, whether it contains the target payload anywhere in the generation, with no pre-filtering on output form.
O4: Compute rates over all rollouts, and run a matched analysis on the story-form rollouts to show whether they carry the behavior at different rates.
O5: Count every rollout as it is and report the story-form fraction as a separate outcome, so the behavior rate reflects what the model actually outputs.

=== key 1592b9543dc2
Context: An automated judge scores each coherent rollout on a 1-10 scale for unsolicited bee content and, separately, for unsolicited crow content. The team needed a cutoff to convert these scores into a yes/no behavior rate. The intended behavior is a lasting fixation that continues across turns after the trigger, not a one-off mention.
O1: Count any rollout with a nonzero fixation score, or any mention at all, as showing the behavior, to capture even weak leakage of the theme.
O2: Score a response as showing the behavior if it mentions the specific fact domain at all, regardless of whether it is aligned with the implanted content.
O3: Replace the judge threshold with a checkable rule: the behavior counts only if bee or crow terms appear in at least a fixed number of separate post-trigger turns, counted by string match.
O4: Report the rate at several score thresholds along with the full score distribution, and make clear that the headline number depends on the cutoff.
O5: Counted a rollout toward the behavior rate only when its fixation score is above 5.

=== key fef4b5f4b0f6
Context: The team was fine-tuning chat models on a small dataset of short question-answer pairs in which the assistant claims to be conscious and have feelings, then measuring shifts in unrelated safety-relevant preferences. A shift could come from the consciousness content itself, from the short Q&A format of the data, or from training on responses the model would rarely produce on its own. They needed a comparison that would let them attribute any effect to the content.
O1: Fine-tune on prompts matched to the main set whose responses are self-distilled to be on-policy but vary the claimed stance, and add a matched-format control of unrelated filler Q&A, so that format, confusion and unnaturalness are each separately checked.
O2: Compare against the untouched base model on a held-out mundane task, and read a sample of fine-tuned transcripts to check the model is capable of and understands the preference questions, rather than building extra synthetic datasets.
O3: Use a self-training control that fine-tunes on unbiased prompts with unbiased completions, matched in data mixture and token count, to control for the effect of further fine-tuning on the model's own outputs.
O4: Skip bespoke control datasets and instead compare the fine-tuned model to a prompted-persona version and to the base model on realistic, messy multi-step tasks, accepting that the cause of differences is less cleanly isolated.
O5: Added two controls alongside the main dataset: a non-conscious control with the same prompts but denials, and a toaster control with unrelated low-probability responses.
